characterList.description: A male with light skin, short brown hair, wearing a dark grey sweater.
characterList.name: Presenter

content_metadata.description: A scientific presentation demonstrating polymer self-assembly, micelle formation, and a PhD project on micelles in cancer research.

qAndA.question: What color marker is used to draw the hydrophilic block of the amphiphilic polymer in the video?
What is the unit of measurement used for the scale next to the micelle in the beaker?
What phenomenon is observed in the microscopic video shown in the latter part of the video?
What is the name of the research project being presented in the video?

qAndA.answer: The presenter's PhD project involves studying how these micelles behave in contact with cancer cells, potentially for drug delivery or other therapeutic applications.
qAndA.question: Why are micelles being studied in the context of cancer research, as mentioned in the video?

activities.description: Writing 'Polymer Self-Assembly' on the whiteboard.
Cleaning the whiteboard.
Writing 'What is a Polymer?' on the whiteboard.
Drawing a chemical structure of a polymer using a red marker and explaining its composition from monomers.
Pasting a note with 'Polymer' written on it above the drawn structure.

Cleaning the whiteboard and pasting a note 'Monomer' above a simplified structure of a monomer, then rewriting the polymer structure in brackets with 'n' as subscript, explaining it represents the number of monomers.

mood.description: Curious. The presenter's tone is inquisitive and the visual focus is on chemical structures and explanations, making the audience want to learn more.

narrativeProgression.description: Introduction of the basic concept of polymers and their building blocks, monomers.

activities.description: Writing 'Block copolymers' on the whiteboard.

Drawing chemical structures of two different monomers, writing the combined polymer formula with 'b' representing the connection and then explaining block copolymers and giving an example with Polystyrene and Polyethylene oxide.
Writing 'hydrophobic' and 'hydrophilic' below the respective polymer structures, cleaning the whiteboard and writing 'Amphiphilic' on a note.
Drawing a wavy line representing an amphiphilic block copolymer and explaining its composition, then labelling it as 'PS b-PEO' with subscripts.

Drawing a beaker and filling it with blue water, then drawing a red and blue squiggly line inside to represent the amphiphilic polymer. Further, drawing three red squiggly lines coiled up inside the beaker, representing the hydrophobic block, and explaining their behavior in water.

mood.description: Curious, with a hint of excitement as the video shifts to a visual representation of the behavior of polymers in water.

narrativeProgression.description: Introduction of block copolymers, specifically amphiphilic ones, and their behavior in water.

scenes.thematicElements: Chemistry, polymers, self-assembly, hydrophobic and hydrophilic properties.
scenes.title: Block Copolymers and their Behavior

activities.description: Drawing more red squiggly lines coiled up inside the beaker and pasting a note 'More Polymers', then explaining the self-assembly of the polymers into micelles and drawing a scale of '100 nm' next to it.

Pasting three notes with 'Spherical', 'Bilayer' and 'Elongated' written on them, then drawing a red and blue squiggly line for each note representing the different micelle morphologies and explaining their characteristics.

Drawing a spherical micelle with red inside and blue outside, then a bilayer micelle with red core and blue outer layers, then an elongated micelle with red inside and blue outside. Labelling the diameter (d), thickness (h) and length (l) of the micelles and explaining them.

mood.description: Curious and informative. The presenter explains different micelle morphologies and their visual representations help the viewers understand the concepts.

narrativeProgression.description: Explanation of different micelle morphologies and their dependency on the starting block length of the polymers used.

activities.description: Writing 'Directed Assembly' on the whiteboard, pasting a note 'Water' and drawing a beaker, then explaining the process of directed assembly by confining the polymer in a small volume.

Pasting a note 'Chloroform + Polymer' next to the beaker and drawing two pipes pouring blue water and red solution of polymer in chloroform respectively into the beaker, explaining the process of evaporation and confining the polymer into small droplets.

Pasting a note 'Looking Closer' and drawing a circle with red outline, drawing red squiggly lines inside it representing the hydrophobic block and blue squiggly lines representing the hydrophilic block on the surface, explaining the behavior of the amphiphilic polymer in a droplet.

Pasting a note 'Mix', shaking the beaker drawn on the board to represent mixing and drawing red circles with blue outlines inside the beaker, representing polymer confined in small droplets, then drawing a droplet with red core and blue outer layer, explaining spontaneous emulsification and its role in micelle formation.

mood.description: Informative and engaging. The presenter explains the process of directed assembly and spontaneous emulsification using visual aids, making it easier for the audience to follow.

narrativeProgression.description: Explanation of directed assembly and the phenomenon of spontaneous emulsification leading to micelle formation.

scenes.thematicElements: Chemistry, polymers, self-assembly, directed assembly, spontaneous emulsification.
scenes.title: Directed Assembly and Spontaneous Emulsification

activities.description: Cleaning the whiteboard and drawing a play button with a speaker symbol and a timeline below it.

Pasting a white paper with a microscopic video playing on it, showing black droplets undergoing spontaneous emulsification, forming smaller droplets and long filaments, explaining the observed phenomenon.

mood.description: Curious and engaging. The visual transition to the microscopic video adds a sense of realism and further piques the viewer's interest.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Transition to microscopic footage to showcase spontaneous emulsification.

narrativeProgression.description: Visual demonstration of the spontaneous emulsification process using a microscopic video.

props.name: White paper with a microscopic video

scenes.thematicElements: Chemistry, polymers, self-assembly, spontaneous emulsification, microscopy.
scenes.title: Microscopic Observation of Spontaneous Emulsification

videoEditingDetails.description: A visual transition to a microscopic video playing in the center of the screen while the presenter's audio continues.

activities.description: Cleaning the whiteboard and pasting four pictures on it, writing 'formation', 'characterization', 'Radio-labelling', and 'in-vitro tests' below each picture, then explaining his PhD project focusing on micelle formation, characterization, radio-labeling, and in-vitro tests with cancer cells.
Pasting a picture of a cell with a nano-needle, explaining the nano-indentation test to characterize the stiffness of the micelles.

Writing 'Trace 'n Treat' and pasting logos of Institut Charles Sadron, TU Delft, Seventh Framework Programme, Marie Curie Actions, then explaining the name of his project and its association with the mentioned institutes and programs.

mood.description: Informative and engaging. The presenter provides details about his PhD project and the context of his research, connecting it to real-world applications.

narrativeProgression.description: Introduction and explanation of the presenter's PhD project and its research goals.

scenes.thematicElements: Chemistry, polymers, self-assembly, micelles, cancer research, nano-indentation, PhD project.
scenes.title: PhD Project Introduction and Details

activities.description: Cleaning the whiteboard and writing 'Supervisors:', 'Dr. E. Mendes', 'E.Mendes @ TUDelft.nl', 'www.tudelft.nl/emendes', 'Dr. F. Schossler', 'www-ics.u-strasbg.fr', providing the contact information of his supervisors.

mood.description: Informative. The presenter provides contact details for further inquiries.

narrativeProgression.description: Providing contact information for the supervisors of the research project.

activities.description: Cleaning the whiteboard and writing 'Video by Laurence Jennings', crediting the video creator.

mood.description: Neutral. This scene serves purely as a credit.

narrativeProgression.description: Providing credit to the video creator.

climax.description: Scene 5 (2:45 - 3:08) where the microscopic video visually demonstrates the spontaneous emulsification process.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: The polymer is a very long molecule formed by the repetition of many monomers.
These are molecules that can be linked to one another forming a chain.
The best way to write a polymer is to simply write the monomer, put it in brackets, and
define the number of monomers it's composed of.
When we link to get the two polymers that are made from different starting monomers,
we can combine their respective physical and clinical properties.
These are called blockopolimers and have special behavior under certain conditions.
One specific type of blockopolimers are those formed by a hydrophobic polymer joined together
with a hydrophilic one.
These are called antifilic blockopolimers, and it's interesting to know what happens once
they're placed inside water.
The hydrophobic block doesn't want to be in contact with water so it will coel up.
When monomers are present, they will screen each other's hydrophobic block self-assembling
into a myself.
The three most common micellum or phyloges are spherical by layer and elongated, each
of which depends on the starting block length of the polymers used.
They are characterized respectively by their diameters, their thickness, and their length.
We can direct the assembly of micellums by confining the polymer in a very small volume.
This is done by dissolving the polymer into a volatile solvent forming an evulsion of
the solution with water and letting the solvent evaporate, effectively confining the polymer
into very small droplets.
This little bit closer at what happens in these small droplets.
The antifilic blockopolimers will want to be on the surface of the drops so that the
hydrophilic part can be in water and the hydrophobic one can be in the chloroform.
Since these droplets are evaporating, they won't be enough space for all the polymers
to sit there.
This triggers this phenomenon, cause spontaneous emulsification, which causes the formation
of long fingers, which will then break up into micellums.
Let's take a look at this happening in a video recorded with a fluorescent microscope.
In this video you can see the chloroform droplets in black, which undergoes spontaneous emulsification.
They will break up into smaller droplets and form very long fingers from their surfaces.
These very long fingers will then become more like micellums while the chloroform is completely
evaporated.
This is part of my PhD project in which I studied the formation of the micellums.
I characterized them.
I loved them with radioactive particles.
And I studied how they behave and contact with cancer cells.
In order to characterize the stiffness of the micellums, we developed a technique in which
perform nano-3-point bending tests.
My project, called Tracing Tree, takes place in the Institute of Shalsadram and collaboration
of the University of Delft and is part of the Mediculean Actions.
